leads.reasoning: Pierce filed amendment #64 opposing Indiana's near-total abortion ban SB1 during the August 2022 special session and argued the bill was 'such bad public policy and just not ready for prime time, that it doesn't make sense to continue.' His amendment was defeated 38-62. He has introduced physician-assisted death legislation (HB1011) for eight consecutive years, reinforcing a strong bodily autonomy position. Record is consistent with keeping abortion legal and broadly accessible.

Pierce served on Indiana's AI legislative task force and opposed a proposed federal moratorium on state AI laws stating 'States need to be able to step up,' but also cautioned: 'If we don't fully understand the potential bad things and we legislate in not the best way, we might stifle some innovation.' This measured pro-oversight stance — favoring disclosure and state-level accountability over banning high-risk uses — maps to new scale 3.

Pierce has advocated for campaign finance reform for over two decades but been blocked by the Republican majority. In a 2022 Journal Gazette article he called out why reform stalls: 'I think because the system is serving them well – when you're in the majority, more donors will contribute to you because you control the fate of their bills.' He brought in experts from Arizona and Maine to an interim study committee to explore small-donor public financing models, placing him firmly in favor of strict limits on corporate donations and dark money.

Pierce consistently cites childcare as one of the three biggest affordability issues facing Hoosiers alongside healthcare and college costs. He has criticized Republican budgets for failing to fund Medicaid waiver waitlists and childcare while providing tax benefits to wealthy families. He supports significant expansion of public childcare assistance as a core economic priority, though he has not explicitly called for a universal public childcare guarantee.

Pierce raised concerns about racial gerrymandering stating Republican maps have 'a very profound impact on the minority voters of Marion County and up in Lake County.' He called IU's arrest of peaceful protesters 'a textbook violation of the First Amendment' (April 2024) and demanded charges be dropped. His record reflects strong civil rights enforcement and opposition to systemic discrimination, though no evidence of reparations support was found.

Pierce opposed SB277 (2026) that prevents Indiana from implementing environmental protections stricter than federal standards, expressing sadness at the legislature's 'lack of commitment to environmental protection.' As ranking member of Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications Committee he has consistently pushed for cleaner energy transition and opposed policies that favor fossil fuel industry interests over public health and ratepayer welfare.

Pierce has been among the most vocal opponents of Indiana's data center expansion legislation. He argued developers and utilities are trying to make local governments 'unable to say no' to data centers despite widespread public opposition. He raised concerns that data centers will drive up electricity bills for ordinary ratepayers and that the 1% local revenue incentive was designed to overcome community resistance. He opposed HB1002 amendments that failed to address data center cost shifting.

Pierce strongly opposed Indiana SB76 (February 2026) requiring state entities to assist ICE, stating: 'Why do we want to give our full, complete compliance to an organization that has proven itself to be poorly trained, incompetent, not able to follow our laws or constitution, and has caused the deaths of innocent U.S. citizens?' He also proposed amendments requiring ICE officers to remove masks during operations. This is consistent with new stance 2 — limiting deportation enforcement to serious violent offenders and opposing broad ICE cooperation.

As ranking member of the Indiana House Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications Committee, Pierce has consistently opposed fossil fuel cost expansion. He expressed sadness that SB277 (2025-26) prevents Indiana from setting stricter environmental standards than federal law, and opposed charging ratepayers for failed nuclear projects. He has opposed data center energy expansion that raises electricity costs for residents. His position favors stopping new fossil fuel permits rather than an immediate ban.

Pierce identifies healthcare affordability as the biggest issue Hoosiers face and describes himself as 'a progressive voice that fights hard to make sure that average Hoosier families have things like health care.' His advocacy focuses on cost regulation and expanding access for working families rather than a fully public system. This aligns with new stance 2 — ensuring everyone has affordable coverage through a mix of public programs and regulated private insurance.

Pierce explicitly opposed SB285 (signed into law March 2026), the bill criminalizing public camping, stating it 'hides the problem of homelessness rather than solving it.' He argued for residential treatment facilities instead of jails, stating jails should not be 'the number one health provider in the community.' He supports fully funded mental health and substance use treatment as the alternative to criminalization.

Pierce opposed SB285 (2026) to criminalize homelessness and instead advocated for residential treatment facilities and wraparound services for people experiencing homelessness. He frames housing affordability as a core issue for average Hoosier families. His record reflects support for targeted government programs and accessible services rather than rent caps or mandates on developers, aligning with new stance 3: offering targeted help such as subsidies for affordable projects and assistance programs.

Pierce introduced an amendment to create an independent nonpartisan redistricting commission, stating 'The eyes are upon us for the moment. We have an opportunity to make a real statement.' He called the Republican gerrymander 'the saddest day I have ever experienced in the Indiana House' and specifically accused the maps of diluting minority voter power. His proposal explicitly removes all elected officials from the mapmaking process.

Pierce has called Indiana's school choice program 'a very deliberate incremental system to divert money away from our public schools,' opposing vouchers for more than a decade. He argues society benefits when public schools bring together all students regardless of class. He has explicitly opposed state budget allocations of 'tax dollars to private or charter schools' and fought universal voucher expansion at every stage.

Pierce has criticized budgets that cut public services like childcare and Medicaid while offering tax benefits to private schools, and opposes utility structures that favor corporate profits. His platform reflects support for moderately raising taxes on wealthy people and corporations to fund existing services for working families — consistent with stance 2 on the new scale.

Pierce directly intervened to kill a transgender bathroom bill in committee by speaking against it to the committee chair, stating 'every little kind of push, and behind-the-scenes discussion that you can do is helpful because that can help maybe stop bad legislation from becoming law.' His consistent opposition to anti-trans legislation places him at the most protective end of the scale.

Pierce introduced an amendment for a nonpartisan redistricting commission and called passage of the Republican gerrymandered congressional map 'the saddest day I have ever experienced in the Indiana House of Representatives.' He serves on the Elections and Apportionment Committee and has consistently supported expanding voter access. His overall record reflects support for broad access to voting including mail-in and early voting expansions.
